accroche: At the Paris Opera, the audience splits into two camps, named after the two corners of the royal box.
contenu_vulgarise:
On August 1, 1752, a troupe of traveling Italian comedians, led by the impresario Eustacchio Bambini, performs at the Académie royale de musique in Paris a short intermezzo by Giovanni Battista Pergolesi, *La Servante maîtresse* (The Maid Turned Mistress). The piece had already been performed in Paris in 1746 without attracting the slightest attention. This time, on the most prestigious stage in France, it sets off a scandal that will occupy Parisian minds for two years.

The Académie royale de musique was the sanctuary of French lyric tragedy, a genre founded by Jean-Baptiste Lully and then exemplified by Jean-Philippe Rameau. Faced with the comic lightness of Italian opera, the Parisian public divides. People get into the habit of naming the two camps after the two corners of the box where the royal family sat at the Opera: the King's corner for the supporters of French music, the Queen's corner for the defenders of Italian opera.

## The battle of the pamphlets

Among the supporters of the Queen's corner is a Genevan philosopher still known mainly as a theorist: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, who himself wrote the articles on music in Diderot and d'Alembert's *Encyclopédie*. In 1753, he publishes his *Lettre sur la musique française* (Letter on French Music), in which he faults Rameau for recitatives that lack, in his view, the naturalness of the Italian's, and for choruses weighed down by learned writing and overly rich orchestration.

His thesis goes even further: the French language itself, he writes, “little suited to poetry,” would be by nature incompatible with music. Rameau answers him with a pamphlet, the *Erreurs sur la musique dans l'Encyclopédie* (Errors on Music in the Encyclopédie), published in 1755. Rousseau, true to his own thesis, will go so far as to write *Pygmalion*, a “lyric scene” premiered in Lyon in 1770, in which the words and the music, rather than combining, are heard one after the other.

## What it shifts

The Quarrel of the Bouffons never really decides between the two musics: French opera continues to be written after 1754, and Rousseau's admiration for Italian opera does not stop him from being the author of operas in French. What the quarrel reveals is something else: that a debate over musical taste, in Paris in the mid-18th century, can mobilize the same pens and the same categories as the great philosophical debates of the time, to the point that an article on singing becomes a ground where the quarrel of the Enlightenment itself is replayed under another name.

citation.texte: I believe our language is little suited to poetry, and not at all to music.

carte.punch: The Paris Opera audience splits into two camps, named after two corners of the royal box.
carte.idee: In 1752, an Italian intermezzo performed at the Paris Opera sets off a two-year quarrel. The audience divides into the King's corner, for French music, and the Queen's corner, where Rousseau defends Italian opera and judges French unfit to be set to music.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The whole quarrel, up to the later birth of French opéra-comique.

quiz.question: Where does the name of the two camps, the “King's corner” and the “Queen's corner,” that clash during the Quarrel of the Bouffons come from?
choix: From the two separate halls where French music and Italian music were performed separately
From the two corners of the Opera's royal box, near which each camp's supporters gathered
From nicknames given by the press to the two main pamphleteers of the quarrel
From the two musicians' guilds, one playing for the king and the other for the queen
quiz.explication: The two camps take their name from the two corners of the box where the royal family sat at the Opera: supporters of French music gathered on the king's side, those of Italian opera on the queen's side. It is neither a separation of halls, nor a press nickname, nor a matter of musical guilds.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which Italian work, performed on August 1, 1752 at the Académie royale de musique, sets off the Quarrel of the Bouffons?
choix: La Servante maîtresse, an intermezzo by Giovanni Battista Pergolesi
Les Indes galantes, an opera-ballet by Jean-Philippe Rameau
Il Trionfo dell'Onore, a comic opera by Alessandro Scarlatti
Castor et Pollux, a lyric tragedy by Jean-Philippe Rameau
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is Pergolesi's intermezzo La Servante maîtresse, given by Bambini's troupe, that sets off the quarrel, even though it had already been performed without success in Paris in 1746.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Rousseau fault in Rameau's music in his 1753 Lettre sur la musique française?
choix: Composing his entire output without respecting any rule of the classical harmony of the day
Unnatural recitatives and choruses weighed down by learned writing and an overly rich orchestra
Never having set a single text by Voltaire or Diderot to music during his career
Borrowing, without saying so, several of his arias from famous Italian composers
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Rousseau faults Rameau for recitatives that lack the naturalness of the Italian's, and for choruses weighed down by learned writing and overly rich orchestration, before extending his criticism to the French language itself.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does Rameau respond in 1755 to Rousseau's criticisms published in the Encyclopédie?
choix: He has the king ban any new Italian opera performance in Paris
He composes a comic opera in Italian to prove his mastery of the rival genre
He publishes a pamphlet, the Erreurs sur la musique dans l'Encyclopédie
He leaves the Académie royale de musique and withdraws from public life
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Rameau answers with a pamphlet published in 1755, the Erreurs sur la musique dans l'Encyclopédie, with no royal ban or withdrawal from public life involved.
